head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of roads at each city
Set of directly connected pairs, stored in both directions
Fast "is there an edge between a and b?"
Roads touching `a` or `b`, counting a shared road twice
A road joining the two cities was counted in both degrees, so subtract it once
Fixing the double count (`True` acts as 1)
Try every pair of different cities

p: The maximum is `4`.

bullets: Space: O(roads) for the set of linked pairs.

1615.takeaway: The rank of a pair is deg[a] + deg[b], minus 1 if the two cities share a road; check every pair.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Start position of the substring in `s` and of the one in `t`
Current length minus one: how far both substrings have been extended
More than one mismatch, and extending can only add more
The pair of substrings of this length differs in exactly one place

p: The total is `3`.

blocks.h: Why does it count each pair once?
p: A pair of substrings is determined by the two start positions and the length. For a fixed pair of starts, the code visits each length once (`k` increases by one), and counts it exactly when the mismatch count is 1.

bullets: Time: O(|s| · |t| · min(|s|, |t|)), which is fine for lengths up to 100.

1638.takeaway: For every pair of start positions, extend both substrings together and count the lengths where they differ in exactly one place.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends at `i`
LIS (Longest Increasing Subsequence) from the left
Length of the longest strictly decreasing subsequence that starts at `i`
The same idea from the right
Mountain length with its peak at `i` (the peak is counted once)
The peak needs at least one element on each side
A mountain cannot be only a slope
Everything not in the best mountain is removed
Minimising removals = maximising what is kept

p: Valid peaks and their mountain lengths: index 3 gives 4, index 4 gives 5, index 5 gives 3, index 6 gives 4. The best is `keep = 5` (for example `1,5,6,3,1`), so the answer is `8 − 5 = 3`.
If `left[i] == 1` the peak has nothing rising before it, and the "mountain" would be just a decreasing run, which is not allowed. The same holds for `right[i] == 1`.

1671.takeaway: Compute the longest increasing run ending at each index and the longest decreasing run starting there; the best peak maximises their sum minus one.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of bits in the binary form of `i`
The width of the number being appended
Shifts the string built so far left to make room for `i`
Puts the bits of `i` into the freed low bits (same as adding here, because those bits are zero)

p: The result is `27`, the value of `11011`.

blocks.h: Why can we take the modulus at each step?
p: Shifting left is multiplication by a power of two, and OR-ing `i` into the freed low bits is the same as adding `i`. Multiplication and addition give the same remainder whether you reduce at every step or only at the end, so reducing each time keeps the numbers small without changing the result.

1680.takeaway: Build the answer incrementally: shift left by the bit length of i, add i, and reduce modulo 10^9 + 7.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The values currently inside the window
The new value `x` is already in the window, so shrink from the left until it is gone

blocks.h: Why does shrinking only from the left work?
p: Values are positive, so a longer window always has a bigger sum than any window inside it. For each right edge we want the longest window of distinct values, which is the one with the smallest valid `left`. When the window breaks, increasing `left` is the minimal change that fixes it.

bullets: Time: O(n), each element enters and leaves the window once.

1695.takeaway: Slide a window of distinct values, shrinking from the left on a duplicate, and track the largest window sum.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Remove every substring `ab` (using a stack) and add `val` for each one
Cancelling adjacent pairs, like matching brackets
The top of the stack is `a` and the new character is `b`, so they form the pair
The stack always holds characters that have not formed a pair yet
Remove the pair and score it
Remove the more valuable pair type first
Remove the other pair type from what is left
The remaining characters can still form the cheaper pair

p: `s = "cdbcbbaaabab"`, `x = 4` (for `ab`), `y = 5` (for `ba`). Since `y > x`, remove `ba` first.
The total is `19`.

blocks.h: Why remove the more valuable pair first?
p: Both kinds of pair compete for the same letters. A removal of the more valuable pair scores more than one of the cheaper pair, and each removal uses up one `a` and one `b` either way, so taking the valuable pairs first and the cheaper pairs from the leftovers gives the best total.

1717.takeaway: Greedily strip the higher-value pair with a stack, then strip the other pair from what remains.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Moves and their opposites; `back` lets the robot return to the previous cell
Exploring and then undoing a move
Set of open cells found so far, in coordinates relative to the start (the start is `(0, 0)`)
The real grid is unknown, so we build our own map
Depth-first search (DFS) that explores every reachable open cell
Asks whether a step is possible
The only way to see walls
Step in, explore, then step back so the robot is at `(x, y)` again
Coordinates of the target if `isTarget()` was ever true
Shortest path in an unweighted grid
Once the map is known, ordinary BFS gives the minimum steps

p: Hidden grid `[[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]]` with start top-left. The DFS maps seven open cells, target at relative `(2,2)`. BFS distances from `(0,0)`:
The answer is `4`.

You cannot run BFS on cells you have not seen, and the robot can only move one step at a time. DFS with backtracking explores the whole reachable region safely (each cell is entered once). BFS on the recorded map then finds the shortest route without moving the robot.

bullets: Time: O(m · n), every open cell is visited a constant number of times.
Space: O(m · n) for the map, the queue and the recursion stack.

1778.takeaway: Explore the hidden grid with DFS and backtracking to build a map, then run BFS on the map to get the shortest path.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Increase in a class's pass ratio if one more student is added: `(p+1)/(t+1) − p/t`
Measuring the benefit of one more unit
Max-heap by gain (Python's heap is a min-heap, so the gain is negated)
Take the class with the biggest gain, add a student, recompute its gain, put it back
Average ratio over all classes, rounded to 5 decimals

p: `classes = [[1,2],[3,5],[2,2]]`, `extraStudents = 2`.
Final ratios: 3/4, 3/5 and 2/2 sum to 2.35, and the average is `0.78333`.

Adding a student to a class helps less and less each time (the gain decreases as the class grows). Because the gains only shrink, always spending the next student where the gain is currently largest is optimal.

1792.takeaway: Use a max-heap on the marginal gain of one more passing student and hand out the extra students one by one.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: With 1, 2 or 3 prime factors, the best count is `n` itself
Fast modular exponentiation: 3 to the power `n // 3`, computed mod 10^9 + 7
Splits `n` into as many 3s as possible, with a leftover of 0, 1 or 2
A leftover of 1 is wasted, so merge it with one 3
Keep the leftover 2 as its own part

p: If `n` has primes with exponents `e1, e2, ...` adding up to `primeFactors`, the number of nice divisors is the product `e1 · e2 · ...`. We want the best way to split `primeFactors` into parts with the largest product.

Splitting a part of 4 or more never lowers the product (`4 = 2 + 2` gives `2 · 2 = 4`, and `5 = 2 + 3` gives `6 > 5`), and three 2s are worse than two 3s (`2 · 2 · 2 = 8 < 3 · 3 = 9`). So use as many 3s as possible and handle the remainder as in the table above.

bullets: Time: O(log n) for the modular power.

1808.takeaway: The count of nice divisors is a product of exponents, so split primeFactors into 3s (with a 2 or 2·2 for the leftover) and use fast modular power.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Any zero makes the product zero
Each negative number flips the sign

p: Four negatives, so the result is `1`.
Only the sign matters, and multiplying 1000 numbers up to 100 in size would create a huge number. Counting negatives gives the answer without overflow.

1822.takeaway: Return 0 if any zero is present; otherwise the sign depends only on whether the number of negatives is even or odd.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Restrictions in position order, with building 1 fixed at height 0
Treating the first building as a restriction
If the last building has no restriction, its height can be at most `n − 1` (starting from 0 and rising by 1 each step)
Adding the far end as a restriction
A limit may not be more than the previous limit plus the distance
The same from the right side
Highest peak between two neighbouring restricted positions `p < q` with limits `hp`, `hq`
The tallest "tent" shape between two points

p: `n = 5`, `restrictions = [[2,1],[4,1]]`. After adding `[1,0]` and `[5,4]`:
The answer is `2`.

head: Pass
Detail
Heights at positions 1, 2, 4, 5
rows: restrictions plus the two added ends

p: Between positions `p` and `q` heights can rise at slope 1 from `hp` and fall at slope 1 toward `hq`. The two slopes meet at height `(hp + hq + (q − p)) / 2`, rounded down because heights are integers. The two passes first make sure `hp` and `hq` are themselves reachable.

bullets: Time: O(r log r), where `r` is the number of restrictions (sorting).

1840.takeaway: Tighten all restrictions with a left-to-right and a right-to-left pass, then compute the highest peak between each neighbouring pair.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Answer queries in increasing order so intervals only ever need to be added
Add an interval that has started, keyed by its size
Lazy deletion from the heap top
The smallest remaining interval contains `q`; otherwise `-1`
Offline answers must be mapped back

p: The answers in the original order are `[3,3,1,4]`.

blocks.h: Why is it enough to look only at the heap top?
p: Every interval in the heap has already started (`left <= q`). Once the expired ones are removed from the top, the top is the smallest interval that is still alive, which means it contains `q`. Expired intervals deeper in the heap are removed later, when they reach the top.

1851.takeaway: Sweep the sorted queries, push started intervals into a size-keyed heap, drop expired ones from the top, and read the smallest.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Equal values become adjacent and values are in ascending order
How many distinct smaller values lie below the current one
Position of the value in the distinct sorted list
This element must be reduced `rank` times, one step per smaller distinct value

p: The answer is `3`: the value 5 goes down `5 → 3 → 1` (2 operations) and the value 3 goes `3 → 1` (1 operation).

One operation lowers one element to the next smaller distinct value. An element with `rank` distinct values below it has to step down through each of them, so it needs exactly `rank` operations, and the operations of different elements are independent in total.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for sorting.

1887.takeaway: Sort, and add to the answer the number of distinct smaller values below each element.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The session crossed midnight, so the logout belongs to the next day
Round the login time up to the next multiple of 15 (the first round that starts after you arrived)
Round the logout time down to a multiple of 15 (the last round that ended before you left)
Number of whole 15-minute rounds between the two, never negative

p: `loginTime = "09:31"`, `logoutTime = "10:14"`.
If you log in and out inside the same round, rounding the start up and the end down can leave `end < start`. The result must be `0` in that case, not negative.

1904.takeaway: Convert to minutes, move the start up and the end down to multiples of 15, and count the whole rounds in between.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The two halves of the string
The win condition compares the halves
Sum of the known digits in each half
How much is still to be decided
An odd number of `?` means Alice makes the last move and can always unbalance the sums
Parity of the number of moves
Bob wins only when the two sides can be made equal under optimal play; otherwise Alice wins

p: `14 != 18`, so Alice wins and the result is `True`.

blocks.h: Why does the formula look like that?
p: When the number of `?` is even, Bob can answer each of Alice's digits `d` with a digit `9 − d` on the same side, so each pair of `?` is worth 9 in total, or 4.5 per `?` on average. Bob wins exactly when `sum_l + 4.5 · q_l == sum_r + 4.5 · q_r`. Multiplying by 2 gives the check `2 · (sum_l − sum_r) == 9 · (q_r − q_l)`, and Alice wins when it does not hold.

1927.takeaway: Alice wins if the number of ? is odd; otherwise Bob wins only when twice the known difference equals 9 times the difference in ? counts.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `for d in range(1, n + 1) if n % d == 0`
Counts how many divisors there are
Counting items that satisfy a condition

p: Three divisors (1, 2, 4), so the result is `True`. For `n = 2` there are only two, so `False`.
A number has exactly three divisors only when it is the square of a prime (like 4, 9, 25). With the small limit, counting divisors directly is simple and fast enough.

1952.takeaway: Count the divisors by trial and compare with 3.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The best group of `k` scores is always `k` neighbours in sorted order
Highest minus lowest in the window of `k` sorted scores starting at `i`

p: The smallest difference is `2`.

blocks.h: Why must the chosen scores be adjacent after sorting?
p: If you pick `k` scores that skip a value in between, replacing the skipped-over extreme with that in-between value keeps or reduces the spread. So some set of `k` consecutive sorted values is always at least as good.

1984.takeaway: Sort, then slide a window of size k and take the smallest max − min.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Greatest common divisor of the sides
The ratio in lowest terms, an exact key for "same ratio"
How many rectangles share each ratio
Number of pairs inside a group of `c`

p: One group of 4: `4 · 3 / 2 = 6` pairs.

Dividing as floating-point numbers can introduce rounding errors, so two equal ratios might not compare equal. The reduced fraction is exact, and two ratios are equal exactly when their reduced fractions are identical.

bullets: Time: O(n log max side) for the gcd computations.

2001.takeaway: Reduce each width/height to lowest terms, group equal ratios, and count pairs per group.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Map from a coordinate to `[height change, count change]`: `+h, +1` where a building starts and `−h, −1` where it ends
Sweep line (processing changes in position order)
Total height and number of buildings covering the segment that starts at the current point
No building here, so this stretch is left out
merge check `res[-1][1] == p and res[-1][2] == avg`
If the previous segment ends here with the same average, extend it
Producing the minimum number of segments

p: The point `9` is the last one and only closes a building, so the loop stops before it (`points[:-1]`).

Building boundaries can split a stretch into pieces that have the same average. The question wants the fewest segments, so if the previous segment ends exactly where this one starts and the average is equal, it is extended instead of adding a new one.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.

2015.takeaway: Sweep over start and end events, keep the running height total and count, and merge adjacent segments that have the same average.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The answer is the largest `k` for which `can(k)` is true; if `k` tasks can be done, so can `k − 1`
If `k` tasks are done, use the `k` easiest tasks and the `k` strongest workers
Best possible choice for a fixed `k`
Tasks the current worker could do if they take a pill, in increasing order
`while ptr < k and ts[ptr] <= w + strength`
Add every task that the worker can reach with a pill
Growing the candidate set as workers get stronger
The worker can do the easiest candidate without a pill
Otherwise take a pill and do the hardest task they can reach
Needed a pill but none left

p: `tasks = [3,2,1]`, `workers = [0,3,3]`, `pills = 1`, `strength = 1`. Check `can(3)`: sorted tasks `[1,2,3]`, workers `[0,3,3]`.
All three tasks are assigned, so `can(3)` is true and the answer is `3`.

blocks.h: Why the weakest worker goes first?
p: The weakest worker is the hardest to place, so it picks first. If it can do the easiest task for free, it should (this saves pills). If not, it must use a pill, and since the pill is spent anyway, it should take the hardest task it can reach, leaving easier tasks for the stronger workers.

bullets: Time: O(n log n + m log m + k log min(n, m)) overall; each check is linear.

2071.takeaway: Binary search the number of tasks; for each guess, match weakest to strongest workers with a deque, using a pill only when needed.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix sums: `pre[i]` is the sum of the first `i` elements
Range sum from two prefix values
Integer division by the window size
Only indices with `k` elements on both sides get an average; others stay `-1`

p: `nums = [7,4,3,9,1,8,5,2,6]`, `k = 3`, so the window has 7 elements.
The other indices keep `-1`, giving `[-1,-1,-1,5,4,4,-1,-1,-1]`.
Recomputing each window would cost O(k) per index. With prefix sums every window sum takes O(1), so the whole job is linear.

2090.takeaway: Use prefix sums to get each window of 2k + 1 elements in O(1) and divide, leaving -1 near the borders.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The last digit is not zero, so no digits are lost when reversing

p: Reversing twice only changes a number if reversing drops something.

blocks.h: Why is a trailing zero the only problem?
p: Trailing zeros become leading zeros after the first reversal, and leading zeros disappear. Every other digit survives both reversals in its original place. Zero itself is fine because it stays `0`.

2119.takeaway: The number survives a double reversal exactly when it is 0 or does not end with 0.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many characters are missing to reach the next multiple of `k` (it is 0 when the length is already a multiple)
Pad the end with the fill character

p: `s = "abcdefghij"`, `k = 3`, `fill = "x"`. The length is 10, and `-10 % 3 = 2`, so two fill characters are added.
In Python the remainder takes the sign of the divisor, so `-10 % 3` is `2`, exactly the amount needed. If the length is a multiple of `k` the result is 0 and nothing is added.

2138.takeaway: Pad the string to a multiple of k with the fill character and slice it into groups of k.
